extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy; general educated readers interested in ethics/psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarises the author's evaluative principles about what determines human will and liberty — focusing on uneasiness, desire, present vs. absent goods, suspension of desire, and the governance of the passions. Useful for close reading, annotation, or philosophical commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uneasiness determines the will
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘uneasiness alone operates on the will, and determines it in its choice’ — the present uneasiness a person feels naturally determines the next action they take.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a person who acknowledges a greater good (virtue, heaven) will not act for it unless they feel an uneasiness (hunger/thirst for righteousness) that compels action. Anti-pattern: relying on mere intellectual assent to a good without any accompanying desire/uneasiness and expecting action to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of Uneasiness is the first Step to Happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Because pain and uneasiness are felt as inconsistent with happiness, the will tends to choose actions that remove present uneasiness as the necessary first step toward happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides explanation of motivation: immediate relief of pain/uneasiness typically takes precedence over pursuing distant goods. Example: people avoid present pain even when a greater future good is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absent goods do not determine the will until made present by desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent goods (future or remote goods) cannot operate on the will unless, by contemplation, they are brought home and raise desire; otherwise they remain bare speculative ideas that do not produce action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: persuasion or information that only presents an abstract good is insufficient; one must cultivate desire (relish) for that good via repeated consideration. Anti-pattern: assuming mere knowledge of a distant good suffices to motivate behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of a great good is insufficient to fix the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the infinitely greater good (e.g., heaven) is acknowledged as possible, its mere possibility would, if absent-goods determined the will, cause constant pursuit; but in fact people neglect it, showing absent possibility alone doesn't determine choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to explain why recognition of moral/religious goods does not guarantee consistent pursuit; practical effect requires present desire/uneasiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: A great present uneasiness holds the will steady
rubrics_metrics.description: Any very great and prevailing uneasiness, once it possesses the will, keeps it steady and intent (e.g., severe bodily pain, impetuous love, desire for revenge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that intensity of present passion can monopolise both thought and action. Example: violent passions prevent deliberation and dominate behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire accompanies (and is often confounded with) uneasiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire is the chief and most sensible form of uneasiness that accompanies voluntary action; the will rarely orders action without some desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains frequent conflation of desire and will. Note that other passions (aversion, fear, anger, etc.) also contain uneasiness and thereby influence the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: The most pressing attainable uneasiness determines next action
rubrics_metrics.description: Among competing uneasinesses, the one most pressing and judged capable of being removed ordinarily has precedence in determining the will for the next action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two constraints: (1) intensity/pressingness, (2) judged attainability. Anti-pattern: pursuing an urgent but judged-unattainable end (which the will will not take as its next object).

rubrics_metrics.name: All desire aims at happiness; goods evaluated by contribution to one's happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire is ultimately for happiness; what each person calls 'good' is what they judge contributes to their happiness, and goods are judged comparatively by degree of pleasure/pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains variability of individual aims: goods valued differ because people include different things as parts of their happiness. Use when analyzing motivational claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only goods considered part of one's happiness move desire
rubrics_metrics.description: A person desires only so much of a good as they consider necessary to make part of THEIR happiness; other goods, however great, do not excite desire if not seen as part of that person's happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: moral appeals must show how the proposed good becomes a component of the individual's conception of happiness in order to motivate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present pains and ordinary necessities limit pursuit of remote goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily uneasinesses (hunger, thirst, cold, fatigue) and habitual desires occupy most of life, leaving little vacancy for attraction to remote absent goods; thus people often choose near satisfactions over distant goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to explain human short-termism and why long-term goods require sustained effort to enter deliberation; policy implication: reduce present uneasinesses or rebalance attention to enable pursuit of distant goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due consideration can raise desire for absent goods
rubrics_metrics.description: By due consideration and examination of a proposed good, one can raise desire in due proportion to its value, thereby bringing it to bear on the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive: cultivation of contemplation and repeated reflection can make absent goods motivationally present. Example: religious meditation or moral education intended to form appetites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to suspend desire is the source of liberty/free-will
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to suspend the execution and satisfaction of any desire, to pause and examine objects of desire before acting, is the hinge of liberty (free-will).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies freedom as the capacity for considered suspension, not indifference. Anti-pattern: equating 'freedom' with impulsive indifference or inability to judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being determined by one's own judgment is consistent with liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: To have one's will determined by the last result of one's own judgment (after due examination) is not a restraint on liberty but its proper exercise; true freedom is acting according to considered judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to counter views that free-will requires being undetermined by reasons; the author argues that rational determination enhances freedom rather than diminishes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater felicity and rational determination increase, not diminish, liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Superior beings (perfectly happy) are more steadily determined by the good yet remain free; being constrained by the pursuit of true happiness is not a loss of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual point useful in debates about compatibilism: determinateness by good does not negate freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense, deliberation, and scrutiny are obligations given inclination to pursue happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Because our inclination to happiness can mislead, we are necessarily put upon caution, deliberation, and examination to ensure particular desires align with our true happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative claim: prudent agents should suspend satisfaction until they have informed themselves as the weight of the matter demands. Application: moral education, personal discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Govern the passions to allow reasoned examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderation and restraint of passions so that the understanding can examine are the right improvement of liberty; one should form appropriate relishes for true intrinsic good by due consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive: cultivate self-control and make resolutions; avoid letting violent passions entirely preclude deliberation. Example: discipline in presence of temptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of pursuits explained by differing conceptions of happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Varied and contrary choices among people do not show absence of pursuit of good; they show that different people place their happiness in different things (study vs. hunting, sobriety vs. debauchery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains moral pluralism and caution against assuming uniform standards of good; use when interpreting differing life aims as coherent rather than irrational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of choosing what makes one miserable: bodily pain and wrong judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Men sometimes choose what makes them miserable either because of (1) pressing bodily pains that force different courses, or (2) wrong desires arising from wrong judgments (particularly about future goods/evils).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic rubric: distinguish choices caused by external necessity (pain, coercion) from those due to mistaken appraisal of future consequences. Application: tailor remedies—alleviate pain vs. correct judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present goods are judged rightly; errors concern future good/evil
rubrics_metrics.description: When only present happiness/misery are considered, a person never chooses amiss; mistakes commonly stem from erroneous judgments about future consequences and what will be necessary for happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic point: corrective education should focus on improving forecasting and judgment about long-term consequences rather than disputing present tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misjudging what is necessary for one's happiness prevents desire for greater absent goods
rubrics_metrics.description: People often conclude they can be happy without certain absent goods, so they are not raised to desire the greatest absent goods; this lack of desire leaves the will free to pursue nearer satisfactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains complacency and resistance to moral improvement; solution: show how the absent good is necessary to the person's conception of happiness via sustained reflection and education.
